prize_parts.citation: For methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets with endogenous prices, which made empirical industrial organisation quantitatively operational for merger, antitrust and regulatory analysis.

statement.case_for: Random-coefficients demand estimation (Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes) solved a concrete identification problem: estimating substitution patterns and market power from product-level data when prices are endogenous. About thirty years of use support the claim. The method is routine in merger review, antitrust and regulation, and it has spread into trade, health, environmental and public economics, so its reach goes well beyond industrial organisation. Pakes's work on dynamic industry models, including entry, exit and investment, extends it to dynamics. Few candidates on the shortlist combine this methodological depth, this breadth of use outside the home field, and this clean a core of contributors. On reflection I still place it first, but I now regard B001 as a close alternative. The B001 attribution is cleaner still, and the two cases differ in kind (method versus theoretical framework) rather than in obvious strength.
statement.case_against: Much of the contribution is a method rather than a substantive discovery, and the identification rests on strong assumptions (instrument validity, functional form) that remain debated relative to design-based approaches. Attribution is also imperfect. Bresnahan's and Reiss's foundational empirical-IO work, and the Ericson-Pakes and Benkard dynamic-games contributions, cannot all be honoured under the three-name cap. A BLP-centred citation therefore risks understating the wider structural programme. I also have to take care that the strength of B002 is not just my own preference for tools I know, since I am a macroeconomist who builds computational methods.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B001 first on its clean Grossman-Helpman attribution and deep roots in the field. He also notes that empirical support for protection-for-sale is mixed, and that the committee may prefer to anchor a trade prize on the firm-heterogeneity line.
responses.response: I agree that B001's attribution is cleaner than B002's. Two names with a joint programme is easier to defend than choosing three from a seven-name list. I find the mixed empirical record of protection-for-sale more worrying than Fredriksson does, though. Structural parameter estimates that are sensitive to specification suggest the lasting value is as an organising theory, whereas BLP has been validated by three decades of use in practice. Whether an organising theory of that kind is prize-sized is a judgement, and I keep B001 as my first alternative. I would also not widen the B001 citation to endogenous growth. That goes beyond the ballot's stated discovery, and the committee should not borrow credit from a strand it did not list.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B002 second. He says the contribution has changed antitrust, merger review and measurement of market power. He admits he may weigh industrial organisation more heavily than the wider committee, and asks which of Bresnahan, Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn best represents the core idea.
responses.response: I share his caution about field proximity and have tried to apply the same test as for other candidates: durable change in how research and policy are done, clarity of credit, and maturity. B002 passes on all three, but not overwhelmingly on credit. On his question, the BLP demand framework is the part that is unambiguous, and Pakes anchors the dynamic work, so the trio is the most defensible core. I accept his implicit point that the Bresnahan omission is a real cost rather than a technicality. That is why I do not claim B002 is clearly ahead of B001, only that I rate it slightly higher on breadth of use.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B018 first for its credible designs and explanatory framework on technology, tasks and the local costs of trade. She flags that Dorn versus Katz is a difficult attribution choice and that the shift-share identification has been debated.
responses.response: I see the policy influence and agree the empirical designs are valuable. I rank it lower, seventh, for two reasons beyond the Dorn-versus-Katz choice. First, the task-based framework draws on Levy, Murnane and Acemoglu, who are not among the credited names or are already recognised, so the technology half of the discovery is poorly attributed. Second, the persistence and magnitude of the China-shock effects are still being revised. A prize built on the trade-shock strand alone with Autor, Dorn and Hanson might be defensible. A prize that also credits the task framework, as the ballot's title implies, is harder to cite cleanly.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B001 first. He values the way the Grossman-Helpman work links trade, growth and political economy across fields, and he regards a two-person prize for the joint body of work as coherent.
responses.response: I agree that the pairing is coherent and the influence general. My qualification is that the ballot's discovery is the political economy of trade policy. The growth-and-trade work is a separate, though related, achievement, and combining them in one citation would blur the credit. If the committee wants to reward the pairing's growth contribution as well, that argues for a deliberate choice about the citation. It does not argue for extending it by implication. I also note that the B001 and B030 overlap over Helpman does not affect B002.

uncertainties: Whether the committee should treat B002 as a methods prize and whether that weakens it relative to a substantive-discovery prize such as B001.
Whether Bresnahan (and Reiss) should displace Levinsohn, which would alter the core of the credit; I have not resolved this within the three-name cap.
How strongly the strong identifying assumptions of structural demand estimation should count against it relative to design-based empirical work.
My assessment of B001, B002 and B050 rests on general knowledge, with no independent verification of citation or impact data.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for B002 or the alternatives B001 and B050. My profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn, Grossman, Helpman, Kiyotaki or Moore. My listed co-authors (such as John Hassler and Timo Boppart, who are committee colleagues, and Smith, Ríos-Rull and Violante) are not credited names in the preferred configuration.
